identification.summary: APT1 is the China-based cyber-espionage group that Mandiant exposed in February 2013 and tied to PLA Unit 61398, the 2nd Bureau of the PLA General Staff Department's 3rd Department, based in Pudong, Shanghai [S1][S2][S8]. Mandiant reported that APT1 stole hundreds of terabytes of data from at least 141 organizations across 20 major industries since 2006. It said 87% of those victims were headquartered in English-speaking countries [S1][S2]. In May 2014 the US Justice Department charged five Unit 61398 officers with economic espionage against US nuclear, solar, steel and metals companies and a labor union [S4].
identification.firstObserved: Mandiant: tracked since 2006 [S1][S2]. The 2014 US indictment describes intrusions from 2006 into 2014 [S4].
identification.notes: Also tracked as Comment Crew, Comment Panda, GIF89a and Byzantine Candor [S8]. Microsoft's public naming map has no Typhoon name for APT1, Comment Crew, Comment Panda or Unit 61398 (checked 2026-10-14) [S10]. Later activity reusing APT1 tooling (Siesta in 2014, Oceansalt in 2018) was not firmly attributed to APT1 by the reporting vendors; see campaigns and gaps [S5][S6].

attribution.sponsor: People's Republic of China, People's Liberation Army: Unit 61398, 3rd Department of the General Staff Department (per Mandiant and the 2014 US indictment) [S1][S4].
attribution.confidence: Mandiant stated that the scale and duration of the attacks from a single group based in China 'leaves little doubt about the organization behind APT1' [S2]. The US government formally charged five named Unit 61398 officers in May 2014, which Attorney General Eric Holder called the first charges of their kind against a state actor [S4]. China's Defense Ministry denied the accusations and called the report 'unprofessional' [S9]. Some independent commentators, such as Jeffrey Carr, argued that Mandiant did not prove APT1 is Unit 61398 [S8].
attribution.basis: Mandiant traced APT1 activity to four large networks in Shanghai and linked it to Unit 61398 using infrastructure and persona analysis [S1][S2]. DOJ indictment allegations, which name Wang Dong, Sun Kailiang and Wen Xinyu as hackers and Huang Zhenyu and Gu Chunhui as managers of supporting infrastructure [S4].

objectives: Long-term, large-scale theft of intellectual property and confidential business information from foreign organizations, chiefly in English-speaking countries [S1][S2]. The 2014 indictment alleges the stolen information benefited Chinese state-owned competitors. Several victims had filed trade complaints against Chinese rivals [S4].

sectors: Steel and specialty metals (U.S. Steel, Allegheny Technologies) [S4]
regions: United States (115 of the victims Mandiant counted, per press coverage) [S11]
15 countries in total, per press coverage of the Mandiant report [S11]
targeting.notes: Mandiant counted 141 victim organizations across 20 major industries [S1][S2] and said its visibility was probably only a small fraction of APT1's total activity [S2]. Sectors from the possibly related Siesta (energy, defense, telecom) [S5] and Shady RAT [S7] campaigns are left out of this list because attribution to APT1 is unconfirmed.

capabilities.summary: Mandiant described a mature, high-volume operation. Average dwell time in victim networks was 356 days and the longest was 1,764 days [S2][S3]. In one case APT1 took 6.5 TB of compressed data from a single organization over ten months [S2]. Its infrastructure included at least 937 command-and-control servers on 849 IP addresses in 13 countries, mostly registered in China (709) and the US (109) [S2]. The 2014 indictment separates hands-on-keyboard intrusion operators from personnel who managed domain accounts and other infrastructure [S4]. Its custom malware (for example Seasalt, circa 2010) was later partly reused in Oceansalt [S6]. The tool and technique list comes from MITRE ATT&CK G0006 separately.

campaigns.name: Start of APT1 activity tracked by Mandiant
campaigns.summary: Mandiant traces APT1 intrusions back to 2006. The indictment's intrusion window also begins in 2006.

campaigns.name: Operation Shady RAT (possible link)
campaigns.summary: McAfee disclosed a five-year campaign starting in 2006 against 72 organizations in 14 countries, including US, Canadian and South Korean government agencies, defense contractors and Olympic committees. McAfee named no actor. Dell SecureWorks later reportedly linked it to the same attackers as APT1.

campaigns.name: Mandiant APT1 report
campaigns.summary: Mandiant publicly attributes APT1 to PLA Unit 61398, citing 141 victims and 20 industries. China's Defense Ministry denies the accusations.

campaigns.name: Siesta campaign (possible link)
campaigns.summary: Trend Micro reported a spear-phishing campaign against energy, defense and telecom targets. FireEye assessed that either APT1 or another group reusing its tools and tactics was responsible.

campaigns.name: US indictment of five Unit 61398 officers
campaigns.summary: DOJ charges Wang Dong, Sun Kailiang, Wen Xinyu, Huang Zhenyu and Gu Chunhui with hacking Westinghouse, SolarWorld, U.S. Steel, Allegheny Technologies, Alcoa and the United Steelworkers.

campaigns.name: Operation Oceansalt (APT1 code reuse, not attributed to APT1)
campaigns.summary: McAfee reported five waves of espionage against South Korea, the US and Canada. Korean-language spear-phishing lures referenced South Korean public infrastructure projects. The Oceansalt implant reused part of APT1's Seasalt code, but McAfee said APT1 was unlikely to have conducted it.

diamond.adversary: PLA Unit 61398 (GSD 3rd Department, 2nd Bureau), Shanghai, per Mandiant [S1][S2]. Five officers were named in the 2014 US indictment [S4].
diamond.capability: Spear-phishing-led intrusions, custom backdoors such as Seasalt, and long-dwell data theft at terabyte scale [S2][S5][S6].
diamond.infrastructure: At least 937 C2 servers on 849 IPs in 13 countries, mostly China-registered. Activity was traced to four large Shanghai networks. Dedicated personnel managed domain accounts [S1][S2][S4].
diamond.victim: 141+ organizations in 20 industries, 87% in English-speaking countries. US industrial firms in nuclear, solar, steel and aluminum, plus a labor union [S2][S4][S11].
diamond.socioPolitical: Economic espionage that allegedly benefited Chinese state-owned enterprises, including firms in trade disputes with victims [S4]. Exposure drove the first US criminal charges against state military hackers [S4].
diamond.technology: Corporate Windows enterprise networks and email holding IP and negotiation data, which can be accessed for long periods without detection [S2][S4].

gaps: The original Mandiant APT1 PDF was not fetched directly (fetches to mandiant/fireeye/lawfare hosts failed). Figures come from a course-site mirror listing and Lawfare and press reproductions [S1][S2][S3].
The DOJ indictment and press release (justice.gov) were not opened. Indictment details come from press coverage [S4].
The APT1 link to Operation Shady RAT rests on a secondary (Wikipedia) citation of Dell SecureWorks. The original Secureworks analysis was not reviewed [S8].

Siesta (2014) and Oceansalt (2018) are tooling overlaps only: FireEye allowed for a copycat, and McAfee judged APT1 unlikely to be responsible. Do not count them as confirmed APT1 operations [S5][S6].
No authoritative public reporting was found on APT1/Unit 61398 activity after 2014, or on how the unit was reorganized after the 2015-2016 PLA reforms.
Microsoft has no public name for this actor [S10]. Overlaps with other PRC clusters are not established in the sources gathered.
Exact publication dates for some secondary sources are given to the month only.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1 (operational environment): For DoD, key terrain is the defense industrial base and industrial-supply-chain enterprise networks (aerospace, metals, energy engineering), which hold technical IP and negotiation data [S4][S11]. STEP 2 (effects): Average dwell times of nearly a year and terabyte-scale exfiltration mean an undetected intrusion can compromise whole program data holdings [S2]. STEP 3 (threat model): The template is spear-phishing, a custom backdoor beaconing to China-registered C2, long-term persistence, then bulk archive-and-exfiltrate. Separate personnel manage infrastructure [S2][S4][S5]. STEP 4 (COAs): MLCOA is sustained economic and technical espionage against firms tied to PRC industrial or trade interests [S4]. MDCOA is a successor PLA unit or a tool-reusing actor using APT1-style long-dwell access against DIB partners supporting Air Force programs. Old APT1 code may be reused under false-flag ambiguity [S6]. Candidate indicators: long-lived low-volume beacons to China-registered IPs, large compressed archives leaving the network, and spear-phishing lures tied to current business or infrastructure projects [S2][S6].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: APT1 shows that dwell time is measured in months to years [S2]. Treat historical log retention and retrospective hunting as mission requirements. (2) Authorities: The 2014 indictment shows how law enforcement responds to state-military intrusions against private firms [S4]. Coordinate DIB-victim intrusions with DOJ/FBI and DC3 rather than handling them as purely military events. (3) Mission assurance: Theft of contractor IP and program data erodes technological advantage without degrading operations, so include contractor networks in mission-relevant terrain analysis [S4]. (4) Coordination: Code reuse across actors complicates attribution [S5][S6]. Pair technical indicators with multi-source intelligence before naming an actor in operational reporting.

provenance.importedSummary: PLA Unit 61398 (Chinese: 61398部队, Pinyin: 61398 bùduì) is the Military Unit Cover Designator (MUCD)[1] of a People's Liberation Army advanced persistent threat unit that has been alleged to be a source of Chinese computer hacking attacks
